prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: while he lives

outputs.L1:
Here are two ways to polish your text depending on the format you prefer. Both options preserve every detail, image, and emotional nuance of the original while enhancing the flow, vocabulary, and eloquence.

### Option 1: Elevated Poetic Prose (Recommended)
> While he lives, I compile an inventory of the scenes around us: light fractured through a filthy glass pane; a dead pigeon lodged high upon a spiked window ledge; a clear plastic bag suspended above him, heavy with fluid—as if water could extinguish everything living inside a person, which, in truth, it can. 
>
> I sit in a corner of the oncology ward, scrolling through an app that reveals other gay men in this hospital. I exchange messages with a stranger I consider meeting down in radiology, but ultimately I refrain. Instead, I coax laughter from the sick man while he remains conscious, complimenting his hospital gown and the sharp, brutal line of his cheekbones carved out by chemotherapy. 
>
> If only healing were as simple as a magnet drawing the corrupted metals from his body. If only I could compose a finer catalog—one richer in magic, less encumbered by roundabout language, truly restorative. If only I had met that stranger in the basement, allowing our shared pleasure to rise through the floors like a soothing poultice of bliss for the sorrow-skinned who sit here, half-lucid and tethered to machinery. 
>
> While he still lives, all I can do is document the vast, tragic landscape of his illness. When he is gone, I am counting on the good memories to come flooding back: his beard a collapsed country where I might seek refuge; his laughter a memory so fluid that I will hear it whenever someone opens a window to scatter the birds.

---

### Option 2: Refined Literary Free Verse
> While he lives, here is the inventory:  
> light trapped in filthy glass,  
> a dead pigeon atop a high, spiked window,  
> a clear plastic bag suspended above him, filled with fluid—  
> as if water could extinguish everything inside a person,  
> and indeed, it can.  
>
> In the corner of the cancer ward, I scroll through an app  
> tracking other gay men in this building.  
> I exchange messages with a stranger I might meet in radiology,  
> but refrain. Instead, I make the sick man laugh while he is awake,  
> praising his gown and the new, severe cheekbones  
> brought forth by chemotherapy.  
>
> If only recovery were as simple as a magnet  
> drawing the bad metals from his blood.  
> If only I could construct a finer list—  
> more magical, less periphrastic, truly restorative.  
> If only I had met that stranger in the basement,  
> our pleasure rising through the hospital,  
> a balm of bliss for the sorrow-skinned  
> who sit half-conscious, half-machinery.  
>
> While the sick man lives, all I can do  
> is recount the vast pastoral of his decline.  
> When he is gone, I am counting on the good to flood back:  
> his beard a ruined country where I will seek shelter;  
> his laugh a memory so liquid  
> I will hear it whenever a window opens to startle the birds.
outputs.L2:
During the time he remains alive, I record a series of observations: light filtering through a grime-covered glass pane, a lifeless pigeon resting on a high window ledge fitted with anti-bird spikes, and a transparent bag of liquid suspended over him—a reminder that fluids possess the power to destroy a body’s inner life, as they indeed can. 

Seated in a corner of the oncology department, I tap through a mobile application to find other gay men within the medical center. I exchange messages with a user I consider encountering in the imaging department, though we never actually meet. Instead, I focus on entertaining the ailing man while he remains awake, offering kind remarks about his hospital garment and his newly sharp, prominent cheekbones that surfaced following chemotherapy. 

I wish healing were as straightforward as using a magnet to draw harmful materials out of his body. I wish I could compile a far better inventory—one infused with true magic, free from indirect phrasing, and genuinely capable of restoration. I also wish I had encountered that unknown man on the lower floor, imagining our shared physical joy ascending through the facility to act as a comforting compress for the grief-laden patients resting in a state of partial awareness and bound to equipment. 

As long as the sick man stays alive, my only capacity is to detail the extensive environment of his disease. Once he passes, I am relying on joyful recollections to return in full force. I will seek shelter within the memory of his facial hair—likened to a fallen territory—and his laughter will linger as such a fluid, enduring recollection that I will perceive its sound whenever a window is unlatched to startle birds away.
outputs.L3:
The cancer ward is a study in sterile monotony. Fluorescent lights buzz overhead, casting a harsh, unforgiving glare on the pale linoleum floors and the beige plastic of the medical equipment. I sit in a vinyl armchair beside his bed, watching the slow, rhythmic drip of the IV bag and the profound toll the treatment has taken on his body. He is diminished—his skin translucent, his frame fragile, his once-vibrant presence steadily eroded by the relentless chemistry of the illness. The air carries the sharp scent of antiseptic and quiet despair, a heavy atmosphere where time feels both frozen and rapidly running out.

To escape the suffocating weight of the room, I pull out my phone and open a dating app—a quiet act of self-preservation and a desperate bid for distraction. I adjust the distance setting to its smallest radius, swiping through profiles in search of another queer person somewhere within the grid of this massive building. I imagine a doctor off shift, an overworked nurse in a breakroom, or perhaps another visitor sitting vigil in a room down the hall. In a place dominated by decay and mortality, I look for a fleeting spark of connection, a shared secret in the digital ether to remind myself that life, desire, and identity still exist beyond these walls.

Yet, my attention constantly pulls back to the man in the bed. I put the phone away and reach for his hand, taking its cold, thin fingers in mine. I offer gentle jokes and soft stories, doing everything I can to coax a rasping laugh from him, prizing those fleeting seconds when his old spirit breaks through the haze of medication. As I smooth the hair from his forehead, an irrational longing takes hold of me. I wish for a simple, magical cure—a power to place my hands over his chest, pull the dark rot of the cancer directly out of his body, and cast it away, leaving him whole and restored.

In the quiet hours, this wish blooms into a grander fantasy. I imagine an act of pure, joyful human pleasure—a burst of queer intimacy, alive and pulsing—erupting somewhere inside the hospital’s cold interior. I picture this vitality transforming into a warm, golden tide that rises through the elevator shafts, seeps through the floorboards, and flows through the ventilation ducts. I dream of it washing over every room as a miraculous balm, neutralizing the toxicity, soothing burns, and radiating through every suffering patient until the entire building is cleared of pain and sickness.

Reality, however, settles back in with a cold, unrelenting weight. I am powerless to stop the disease, unable to alter the tragic trajectory of his failing health. Stripped of control, I choose to bear witness. I begin to document everything—the faint rhythm of his pulse, the quiet cadence of his breathing, the specific warmth of his skin when the afternoon sun hits the window. I record these days meticulously, relying on the hope that when he finally passes away, these saved moments and cherished memories will become a lasting refuge, preserving the light of who he was long after he is gone.
outputs.L4:
The air in Room 412 is heavy with the scent of rubbing alcohol, stale tea, and an unmistakable, quiet stillness. Sitting in the vinyl armchair beside the bed, I find myself anchoring my mind to the only things that seem solid: the stark, clinical details of the room. I count them like a Rosary of the mundane. Three IV bags hanging like strange fruit from a metal tree. A pale yellow privacy curtain suspended from a rusted track. The rhythm of the heart monitor, chirping in a steady, cold cadence. A plastic water pitcher with a flexible straw bent at an awkward angle. In a cancer ward, grief does not always arrive as a sudden, tearing storm; often, it begins as a quiet, desperate inventory of an environment designed entirely around the logistics of decline.

When the silence grows too heavy to bear, I reach into my pocket for my phone. My thumb swipes mechanically across the glowing glass—headlines about distant politics, mindless video clips, updates from lives moving forward at normal speed outside these windows. It is a small, pathetic distraction, but necessary. I let the cool blue light fill my eyes, using the digital noise to build a temporary wall between myself and the relentless ticking of the wall clock, which marks down the remaining hours with unfeeling precision. 

Yet, the screen is only a brief reprieve. Looking up, I see the fragile form swallowed by the harsh white hospital linens. Desperate to soften the sharp edges of the room, I lean in close and offer a terrible joke—a callback to a foolish memory from a summer long before the diagnosis. For a fleeting second, it works. A faint, raspy chuckle rises from their chest. It is a fragile sound, stripped of its old strength, but in that brief moment, the suffocating atmosphere of the ward lifts. Humor becomes our frail, beautiful shield, a quiet rebellion against the dark.

In the quiet that follows the laughter, however, a stark realization settles in. There is an immense, heartbreaking boundary to what love can accomplish. I realize that no combination of words, no intensity of desire, and no amount of silent pleading can rewrite the physical trajectory unfolding before me. Language cannot alter the cellular reality of a body surrendering to illness; love cannot hold back the tide. 

And yet, as I sit here watching the slow rise and fall of their chest, a deeper comfort begins to take root beneath the sorrow. This room—with its fluorescent lights, its chemical smells, and its harsh machinery—is temporary. When the end finally comes and the clinical noise fades, these sterile walls will not be what remains. What will return, sweeping over the pain of these final days, are the vibrant years that came before. The warm, resonant sound of their true laughter, the brightness in their eyes, and the irrepressible energy of their life will flood back into the quiet spaces left behind. Death may claim the body, but it cannot claim the history we built; those living memories will endure, offering a lasting emotional refuge that time and loss can never erode.
outputs.L5:
There is a quiet, profound urgency tucked inside the present tense. We so often live as if the people who anchor our lives are permanent fixtures—as enduring as the mountains, as reliable as the rising sun. But time moves with a silent, relentless cadence, reminding us that every moment with those we hold dear is a borrowed gift. 

While he lives, the world carries a specific kind of warmth that cannot be replicated. 

While he lives, history is not merely a collection of dates in a textbook or fading photographs in an album. It is a breathing narrative. His hands—lined with the topography of decades, calloused by hard work and softened by time—still hold the weight of a thousand stories. To listen to him speak is to travel back through time, to hear the echoes of a world that was, shaped by the choices he made and the trials he endured. 

There is an art to loving someone in the autumn of their life. It requires us to slow down, to trade our frantic pace for the quiet rhythm of his days. It means sitting on the porch long after the sun has set, listening to the same story told for the hundredth time, recognizing that the magic is not in the novelty of the tale, but in the cadence of his voice telling it.

Too often, we save our gentlest words, our deepest gratitude, and our highest praise for eulogies. We flower the ground only after the tree has fallen. But gratitude expressed to a tombstone is a echo sent into a void; gratitude offered today is a balm to a living soul. While he lives, there is still time to say the things that matter. There is time to seek his wisdom, to ask for his forgiveness, to offer ours, and to ensure he knows the indelible mark he has left upon our hearts.

While he lives, he remains our sanctuary—a link to our origins, a mirror reflecting where we came from, and a guide for where we are going. His presence provides a subtle comfort, a safety net woven from decades of unconditional love and quiet strength.

One day, the chair will be empty. The room will grow still, and the stories will exist only in our memories. The world will keep turning, but it will feel perceptibly colder, lighter, and less grounded. 

That day will come, as it does for us all. But today is not that day. Today, the sun shines, his heart beats, and his laughter still fills the room. 

So, while he lives, let us honor his presence. Let us hold his hand a little tighter, listen a little longer, and love him with the full measure of our devotion—not in memory of who he was, but in celebration of who he is, right now, in the golden light of the present.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem set in a hospital cancer ward that blends themes of modern queer desire, intense grief, and the surreal textures of serious illness.
counterfactuals.output:
The linoleum reflects the room like a dark, sanitized pond where plastic lotuses float. Under the relentless buzz of the overhead LEDs, your scalp—shaved clean long before the infusions demanded it—rests in the hollow of my throat, smooth as a river stone. The IV pole is an iron spine growing out of the floorboards, its clear tubing a network of glass veins pulsing with a cold, pale poison. The heart monitor counts off the seconds in high-pitched, auto-tuned blips, a slow synth-line for a track no one wants to dance to, yet here we are, shuffling our feet in the dark.

I slide my hand beneath the papery hem of your gown, careful to skirt the rubber port stitched into your chest. There is still the ghost of sweat and poppers locked in the grain of your skin, the memory of the sweat-slicked darkroom where we first pressed our mouths together like a frantic secret. Now, my thumbs trace the faded stick-and-poke star on your hipbone, the flesh beneath it sharp and shrinking, alarming in its heat. Desire in this room is contraband, smuggled past the night station in the pockets of oversized vintage leather, hidden beneath plastic cups of crushed ice. I want to bite the curve of your jaw until you remember you are an animal, not a chart, not a prognosis, not a series of fluid intakes logged into an iPad by a nurse with bored, tired eyes.

Time in 412 expands and curdles like spoiled milk. Outside the double-paned glass, the highway bleeds a steady ribbon of red taillights, but in here, the chemo bag hangs like a translucent jellyfish, glowing with a faint, chemical moonlight. Grief is not a sudden wave; it is a pair of powder-blue latex gloves snapped tight against skin. It is the way you mutter a drag queen’s catchphrase into your pillow between bouts of dry-heaving, your humor a jagged piece of mirror you hold up to blind the room. When you drift into the morphine-haze, calling out for boys we used to kiss in truck beds, I don't correct you. I dip a pink foam swab into ice water and wet your cracked lips, feeding you liquid like a desperate priest serving communion to a god who is unlearning his own name.

We are too young for the room to smell this much like rust and crushed carnations. When the hallway finally goes quiet, I climb over the side-rail and crawl into the narrow, mechanical bed, fitting my body around your frail geometries, wedging myself between your fragile ribs and the hum of the air purifier. I press my mouth to the pulsing blue vein at your temple, tasting copper and salt. You open your eyes, dark and dilated as a midnight alleyway, and whisper, *touch me like I’m still real.* So I do. I put my hand over your quiet heart and pull you close, anchoring us both to the linoleum floor, while above the drop-ceiling panels, an unseen choir sings a slow, distorted pop song, and the sterile world dissolves into the terrible, blinding light of how much I love you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a raw, contemporary piece about sitting with a loved one undergoing chemotherapy? Include specific details about checking a location-based hookup app while by their bedside, feeling helpless, and trying to make them laugh. Format it as a single continuous block of prose poetry.
counterfactuals.output: The fluorescent light humming above us is the exact frequency of a migraine, casting a flat, greenish glaze over the vinyl chair, the linoleum, the terrible starkness of your knuckles where the tape pins the cannula to your vein. I am holding your left hand, warm on top, icy beneath, listening to the IV pump count out its slow, mechanical rhythm—drip, beep, drip—as the poison creeps in to do its quiet, violent work. I feel so utterly hollowed out, a heavy, useless ghost sitting beside you, incapable of filtering your blood or absorbing a single drop of your fatigue, so while you close your eyes and drift into that pale, drug-heavy fog, my hand slips into my pocket. My thumb acts on its own, a desperate, dirt-brained reflex tapping the app icon, opening the bright yellow grid in the shadow of the bedsheet. *Blake, 300 feet away, masc, host, looking for now.* Someone in the parking garage, or three floors down in orthopedic surgery, looking for friction, looking for an hour of mindless, sweaty proof that a body can still exist without suffering. It feels monstrous, swiping through headless torsos and brutal little bios while your red-bagged chemo bag empties into your chest, but I am drowning in the sterile silence, starved for a reminder of pulse and hunger, terrified by the quiet arithmetic of your cell count. I lock the screen, nauseated by my own pathetic twitch for distraction, and shove the phone deep into my coat. I look at you, at the thin line of your jaw, the blue shadow beneath your lower lip, and the helplessness turns into something sharp and reckless in my throat. I lean in close, past the smell of saline and alcohol wipes, and whisper against your ear, *“Hey, wake up, if you puke on my shoes I’m going down to the lobby to hook up with a guy named Flex who claims he’s a discreet top.”* Your eyelids flutter, a tiny crease forms between your brows, and then your chest heaves—a dry, ragged little cough of a laugh breaks out of you, completely cracking the oppressive silence of the room, your eyes blinking open, glittering with a second of pure, ridiculous life. You call me an idiot under your breath, the small smile staying on your lips just long enough for me to breathe again, before the dark water of the exhaustion pulls you back under, leaving me sitting in the hum, holding your cold hand, my thumb still throbbing with the ghost of a glowing screen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about cancer, grief, and Grindr.
counterfactuals.output:
The oxygen machine clicks like a clock,
a steady, mechanical count to zero.
In the corner chair, under the hospital draft,
my phone glows blue in the dark:
*Looking?*

I scroll through a grid of headless torsos,
smooth, unblemished, impossibly alive—
a bitter contrast to the paper skin beside me,
the IV lines, the morphine drip at five.
On screen, they ask for *host or travel?*
In the room, a soul prepares to fly.

Grief is a vacuum that demands to be filled.
It makes a monster of the lonely heart.
I tap a silhouette three blocks away,
seeking a friction that might pull apart
the heavy, suffocating drape of death,
if only for a temporary start.

I step into the elevator’s sterile glare,
leave the hospice floor, the quiet bed,
and walk into a stranger’s dimly lit apartment,
where nothing of the terminal is said.
He doesn’t know about the stage four diagnosis,
or the white flowers lying by your head.

He thinks my shaking hands are just desire.
He presses his full weight against my chest,
and for twenty minutes, the cancer disappears.
There is no biopsy, no final rest,
only the blunt, chaotic proof of being human,
a brief, warm pulse against the cold unrest.

Then shoes are tied. The quiet *“thanks, man”* comes.
I step back out into the midnight air.
The grid refreshes on the journey back—
a hundred strangers, oblivious and bare.

I swipe it closed and climb back to your room,
where the monitors hum their quiet, steady tone.
I hold your cold, pale hand inside the dark,
and use the warmth I borrowed from a stranger
to keep you from feeling so alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a stream-of-consciousness poem in the style of contemporary queer writers like Richard Siken or Ocean Vuong, focusing on hospital visits, chemotherapy, bodily transformation, and longing.
counterfactuals.output:
The clear bag hangs above us like a jellyfish made of plastic and salt, drip, drip, the cold entering the bend of my elbow, say *flush the line* and mean *kiss me before the room turns to chalk*. There is a math to this place—four corners, twelve beats per minute, the nurse’s gloved fingers walking up my forearm looking for a vein that hasn't collapsed into a bruised violet ribbon. *Hold still, sweetheart.* But I can’t. Your hand is on my knee and it is the only warm continent left on the map. Look at me. Look at what they’re pumping into the basement of my ribs. They call it the Red Devil, ruby-bright and chemical-heavy, toxic as a secret we kept in high school behind the grandstands, but here it’s just medicine, here it’s *open wide, swallow the ice, lean back*.

I want to be a body that doesn't leak light.

I want to bruise you with my mouth instead of these yellowing moons where the butterfly needles bit down. Yesterday my hair came away in the shower like dark wet grass pulled from a garden—you didn't flinch, you just gathered it from the drain, a handful of black thread, and put it in your pocket like a love letter. Is this transformation or subtraction? If you strip away the weight, the hair, the thick muscle of the thigh, if you burn the house down to kill the rat, what stays behind? Just the wanting. Just the wild, stupid, ravenous wanting.

Tell me about the car ride again. Tell me about the radio, the highway running south, the air smelling of pine and cheap exhaust, before the white gowns, before the plastic basins, before my skin turned translucent enough to count the blue wires underneath.

*Breathe in.*
*Breathe out.*

The monitor sings its tiny, sterile psalm. *Beep. Beep.* You lean over the aluminum rail, your forehead against mine, your breath smelling of hospital coffee and cold mints. You press your thumb over the port under my collarbone, that little silver coin buried beneath the flesh, an altar made of plastic and titanium. Touch it. Tell me it belongs to you and not the machine. I used to think love was a boy pressed against a brick wall in the dark, all teeth and leather, but today love is you wiping a stray drop of bile from my chin, love is you kissing my bare, shaved skull and calling it a moon.

Don't let go. The room is tilting into the fluorescent ceiling. The saline tastes like pennies on the back of my tongue.

Kiss me until the poison forgets what it came here to do.
Put your hand on my chest.
Listen.
Prove I am still a river.
Say *stay*. Say *stay*.
Say *open your eyes, baby, look at the sun on the floor, we aren't done making a life out of this.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poem about someone sitting with a dying partner, where the narrator lists sensory details of the room to cope with the reality of impending loss, contrasting the heavy medical setting with fantasies of escape and magic.
counterfactuals.output:
There are forty-two white tiles on the ceiling.
One is stained in the corner, shaped like an island
we promised we would visit when the summer came.
The fluorescent light hums in a steady B-flat.
The floor smells of bleach and artificial lemon.
The vinyl of this armchair creaks whenever I shift my weight.

I count the sensory things to keep from disappearing.
The plastic tube, coiling like a translucent snake from your arm.
The cool, metallic taste of the room’s recycled air.
The rhythm of the monitor—seventy-four beats a minute,
then seventy-two,
a cold, electronic metronome marking down the dark.
Your hand in mine feels like dry paper,
light as a fallen leaf before the frost sets in.

If I look too long at the IV pole, I will break.
So I imagine it is a silver birch tree,
stretching its branches toward a canopy of dark velvet.
I pretend the clear fluid dripping through the line
is liquid starlight, melted down by ancient alchemy,
poured into your veins to give you back your wings.

I try to conjure an escape.
I turn the hiss of the oxygen pump into the sound of a distant ocean,
crashing softly against a shore made of crushed pearls.
I imagine the two of us slipping through the double glass windows,
leaving the sharp tang of antiseptic behind,
flying over the city lights like two sparks caught in a night draft.
We would ride the wind until our lungs filled with wild, cold air,
unburdened by blood pressure cuffs or the heavy algebra of survival.

In my mind, I am an sorcerer rewriting the charts at the foot of your bed.
I rub out the numbers with my thumb and replace them with spells:
*Resurrection. Eternal spring. Time moving backward.*

But then the machine beeps, a sharp, clinical intrusion.
The monitor drops to sixty-eight.
The lemon bleach returns.
The air is cold again, heavy with the quiet terror of 3:00 a.m.

Your thumb twitches against my palm—a faint, dry flutter.
I catch my breath and start the list over again.
One door. Two chairs. Three drips per second.
I hold tight to the facts of this room,
and fight the magic off a little longer,
just to stay here with you in the real world
for one more breath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
